# Deposit banking and bills of exchange (`banking_credit`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by coinage, double_entry, interest_loans_collateral, postal_system
- Core idea: A bank keeps deposits and lends out most of them, holding only a reserve, because depositors rarely all withdraw at once; it pays from one account to another by a book entry, so coin need not move. To pay at a distance, a merchant in Florence pays a banker and receives a bill of exchange: a written order on the banker's correspondent in Bruges to pay a named person a sum in Bruges money on a set date. Bills flow both ways, so the correspondents settle by offsetting and only net balances travel as coin. Minimum design: an honest ledger, trusted correspondents, the owners' own capital at risk, a reserve sized for bad weeks, and loans spread over many borrowers.
- Pitfalls:
  - Lending deposits to one prince: Bardi and Peruzzi of Florence failed in the 1340s after Edward III stopped paying (how much this caused the crash is debated)
  - Lending long with money depositors can withdraw tomorrow: the first rumour starts a run that ruins even a sound bank
  - Treating a bill of exchange as a mere money transfer: with exchange and re-exchange it was often a disguised interest-bearing loan, which is why theologians fought over it
  - Calling fractional reserves a fraud and insisting on 100 % reserve: full reserves against demand deposits still allow fee income and lending from equity or separately raised funds
  - Assuming banking began in Renaissance Italy: Babylonian business houses, Athenian trapezitai, Abbasid jahbadhs and Chinese remittance offices all came earlier
- History: mesopotamia: 2nd millennium BC – temples, palaces and merchants take deposits and lend; c. 600–480 BC the Egibi family of Babylon run a multi-generation business of deposits, loans, payment orders and property; 5th c. BC Murashu house at Nippur finances landholders; greece: 4th c. BC – Athenian trapezitai (table bankers) such as Pasion take deposits, lend and pay on clients' instructions; rome: argentarii take deposits, lend and keep accounts for clients; transfers by written instruction; islamic: 9th–10th c. – jahbadhs (state bankers) in Baghdad; suftaja, a loan repayable in another city, avoids transporting coin; sakk is a written payment instrument. Classical hawala transfers a debt obligation; modern hawala brokers arrange remittances and settle balances between themselves; china: c. 9th c. – Tang feiqian ('flying money'): merchants deposit cash in the capital and redeem the certificate in the provinces; 19th c. Shanxi piaohao remittance banks; india: medieval onwards – hundi, merchant bills for remittance and credit, used across the subcontinent; europe: 12th c. – Genoese bankers' deposit accounts; 13th c. bills of exchange at the Champagne fairs; 1397–1494 Medici bank with branches across Europe; 1401 Taula de Canvi of Barcelona; 1407 Casa di San Giorgio, Genoa; 1609 Amsterdam Wisselbank
- Read:
  - Raymond de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (1963)
  - William N. Goetzmann, Money Changes Everything: How Finance Made Civilization Possible (2016)
  - Charles P. Kindleberger, A Financial History of Western Europe (1984)
